speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In the Worldwide Governance Indicators by World Bank in 2018, Singapore ranked in the 97th percentile for Rule of Law.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In the Global Competitiveness Index published by the World Economic Forum in 2019, Singapore maintained the top position for the efficiency of its legal framework in dispute resolution.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In fact, Singapore has been ranked first, out of more than 140 countries, in this component of the index, every year for the past 10 years.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Singapore has also scored highly for judicial effectiveness in the Heritage Foundation Index of Economic Freedom in 2019.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The Ministry of Law has been working with the Courts to ensure that Court proceedings are efficient and that the quality of justice remains high.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: To this end, for instance, we established the new Family Justice Courts in 2014, with the aim of taking a more multidisciplinary and collaborative approach to family disputes.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We established the Singapore International Commercial Court (SICC) in 2015, as part of our drive to bolster our status as a hub for resolving commercial disputes.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The Office of Transformation and Innovation was also set up under the auspices of the Supreme Court in 2018.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: As part of the overarching Courts of the Future blueprint, it has commenced work on various projects and technological enhancements, with a view to enhancing access to justice, improving processes and also embracing innovative ideas for change.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: One upcoming initiative is the use of videoconferencing for a variety of non-trial hearings.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The current Bills continue in this spirit by facilitating a better use of judicial resources and also introducing procedural amendments to enhance the flexibility and also the efficiency of Court processes.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This will also translate to real and practical benefits for Court users both in terms of time and also costs.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: A key change is the restructuring of the Supreme Court to establish a new Appellate Division of the High Court.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The Court of Appeal is the highest Court of the land.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It hears both civil and criminal matters arising from decisions of the lower Courts and tribunals.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The decisions of the Court of Appeal form a body of authoritative law that has shaped our local jurisprudence.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The Court of Appeal has experienced a growing caseload for both criminal and civil matters.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In 2013, there were 314 civil and criminal matters filed to the Court of Appeal.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Overall, the Court of Appeal heard 56% more matters in 2018 compared to 2013.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In addition to the growing caseload, the Court of Appeal has also observed that the cases it is hearing are becoming increasingly complex.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The Court of Appeal generally sits with no more than three judges to hear each case.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In some of the complex appeals, the Chief Justice may convene an enlarged panel of appeal judges to hear the appeal.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This is to allow difficult or novel issues to be considered with the benefit of the collective wisdom and insight of a larger pool of judges.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: There has been a growing number of written decisions issued by a five-judge bench of the Court of Appeal, which is itself indicative of the jurisprudential significance and difficulty of such cases.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In 2015, by contrast, 4.3% of all reported decisions were issued by a five-judge coram.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: By 2018, this number had increased to about 11.5%.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The increased caseload and complexity of matters have stretched the resources of the Court of Appeal.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Thus far, the Supreme Court has taken interim measures to manage the increasing caseload and also the complexity in the Court of Appeal's docket.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Some of these measures, Members would know, include having more High Court judges sit on Court of Appeal hearings and also increasing the sitting days for the Court of Appeal.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This will allow civil appeals arising from decisions of the existing High Court to be distributed between two appellate courts, namely, the Appellate Division of the High Court – the new Court that is being set up – and the existing Court of Appeal, which will remain.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: These targeted structural reforms to the Supreme Court create a more permanent solution to the issues facing the Court of Appeal.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The reforms will help to address the growing caseload and also allow the Court of Appeal to focus its resources as appropriate.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: First, in terms of the restructuring of the Supreme Court.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Under the structural reforms introduced by the Bills, the Supreme Court will continue to comprise the Court of Appeal, which will remain as the apex Court in Singapore and the High Court.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The High Court will, in turn, be restructured to consist of the General Division of the High Court as well as the Appellate Division of the High Court.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I shall first touch on the General Division, before elaborating on the interaction between the Appellate Division and the existing Court of Appeal.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In essence, the General Division will be the present-day High Court.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: As is the case today, it will include the SICC and also the Family Division of the High Court.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Any originating case, appeal, stated case or other recourse which presently lies to the existing High Court will continue to lie to the General Division.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: There will generally be no change to the current position on whether there is further recourse to an Appellate Court.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Hence, if certain decisions of the existing High Court are currently final, then, in most of these cases, those decisions of the General Division will likewise be final.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Similarly, if decisions of the existing High Court are appealable with leave, or appealable as of right, then those decisions of the General Division will likewise be appealable as of right or with leave as appropriate.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The original intention overall is to preserve the status quo with regard to the finality of decisions of the General Division.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Appeals arising from a decision of the General Division will be allocated between the Appellate Division and the existing Court of Appeal.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In general, the Court of Appeal will hear all criminal matters.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It will also hear appeals or processes that are to be heard by the Court of Appeal under written law and prescribed categories of civil appeals.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Where the appeal falls within the categories of appeals prescribed in the Sixth Schedule, then a party should file the appeal or leave application pertaining to that appeal to the Court of Appeal.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Where the appeal is not prescribed in the Sixth Schedule, a party should file the appeal or leave application to the Appellate Division, or otherwise in accordance with written law.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Based on these principles, appeals arising from cases relating to constitutional or administrative law, appeals arising from decisions of the SICC and appeals arising from cases relating to the law of arbitration will ordinarily be allocated to the Court of Appeal.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Those are examples; the list is not exhaustive.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Where a single appeal contains multiple issues, which I think Members would have their own experience with, some issues may fall within the prescribed categories, others may fall outside.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In those situations, the appeal should be filed to the Court of Appeal.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: For example, if an appeal arises from a case relating to constitutional law, but also, as part of the case, raises issues touching issues on contract or tort law, that appeal should be filed to the Court of Appeal.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: All criminal appeals currently heard by the Court of Appeal will continue to be heard by the Court of Appeal.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The Appellate Division will hear all other civil appeals that are not allocated to the Court of Appeal.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The prescribed categories may be amended by the Minister, after consultation with the Chief Justice, by order published in the Gazette.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This will allow for the allocation of appeals between the Appellate Division and the Court of Appeal to be refined and also evolved, taking into account operational experience as well as evolving policy considerations.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And obviously, as I explained earlier, on novel areas, which are currently prescribed, they may, over time, not become novel anymore or it may well become settled with the passage of time.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In those cases, there would be flexibility in moving cases or types of cases in and out of the Sixth Schedule.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The Appellate Division will ordinarily sit as a panel of three Judges.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This reflects its stature and significance as an Appellate Court.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: To provide for flexibility in the arrangements, the Court of Appeal will have the power to transfer to itself any appeal that has been made to the Appellate Division and vice versa.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The Court of Appeal has that power, not the Appellate Division, to transfer cases from the Appellate Division to itself or cases from the Court of Appeal to the Appellate Division.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This can happen, notwithstanding the Sixth Schedule allocation of appeals.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: To give an example, the Court of Appeal may transfer to itself, an appeal which is ordinarily allocated to the Appellate Division, if the appeal concerns a dispute involving complex and novel points of law, and the Court of Appeal is satisfied that it will be more appropriate for the matter to be resolved by an earlier decision of the apex Court, in other words, giving guidance at an earlier stage so that the law becomes settled on a key and important issue.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The Court of Appeal may also consider factors, such as whether there are conflicting judicial decisions on the point of law in question which merits clarification.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Conversely, the Court of Appeal may also decide to transfer to the Appellate Division, an appeal which is ordinarily allocated to the Court of Appeal.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: For instance, an appeal arising from a case relating to constitutional law is ordinarily allocated to the Court of Appeal.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: However, if the General Division has already rendered its decision on the case and the only issue on the appeal is one of costs, for example, then the Court of Appeal may well decide to transfer the appeal to the Appellate Division.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, the overall subject matter may fall within, but the issue at stake between the parties, might well relate to something straightforward.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In that scenario, the Court of Appeal can exercise its discretion to transfer it to the Appellate Division.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: As another example, an appeal arising from a case relating to contempt of Court is ordinarily allocated to the Court of Appeal.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: However, if all issues on appeal relate to uncontroversial points of law, then the Court of Appeal may transfer the appeal to the Appellate Division.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The same principles as I have explained will apply.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Parties themselves may also apply to the Court of Appeal for the appeal to be transferred to the Appellate Division, if the appeal has not been filed to the correct Appellate Court.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: To be clear, after the Appellate Division has issued its decision on an appeal that has been transferred for its determination, it remains possible – although not the usual course – but possible for a party to bring a further appeal to the Court of Appeal.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This will, however, be subject to the fulfilment of stringent criteria that I will come to in a while.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The transfer powers help to ensure that the Court of Appeal's resources are focused on the matters that necessitate a decision from the apex court.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The matters that the Court of Appeal will have regard to, when deciding whether to exercise its powers of transfer, will be set out in the Rules of Court.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This is consistent with the practice in other jurisdictions, such as the United States (US), United Kingdom (UK) and Australia, where there is no automatic right of appeal to the apex Court.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: All such applications for leave will be assessed based on criteria that are more stringent than the usual common law principles that govern applications for leave to appeal against a decision of the General Division.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: To be clear, if you need to seek leave to appeal from the first instance, High Court currently, or the General Division, those principles are fairly settled, I think Members know.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But the principles on which leave will be accessed to be granted for appeals from the Appellate Division up to the apex Court, those would be applied in a far more stringent manner.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Because in those situations, the parties would already have had one round of appeal.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The Court of Appeal may also take into consideration other factors, such as whether a decision of the Court of Appeal, as the apex Court, is required to resolve the point of law and whether the interests of the administration of justice require the Court of Appeal's consideration of that point of law.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: To be clear, so that I do not come across as suggesting that there are automatically three stages, three tiers of Courts, the Appellate Division should not be seen as a further tier of appeal that must be crossed before a matter can reach the Court of Appeal.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Where an appeal lies from a decision of the General Division, then the appeal will lie either to the Appellate Division or to the Court of Appeal.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It will not be commonplace for appeals to be brought to the Appellate Division first and then further brought on to the Court of Appeal.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I hope I have explained that clearly enough.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The Bills also make a number of other amendments to help ensure the timely disposal of appeals, ensure better use of limited judicial resources and bring the overall cost of litigation down.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: First, under existing Court processes, the Court of Appeal will ordinarily sit in a panel of three Judges to hear an appeal or application.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: However, certain applications can be dealt with by one Judge or, in some cases, two Judges.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Certain appeals can also be heard by a panel of two Judges.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We will apply a similar approach to the Appellate Division.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, what I have outlined is the current position.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We will apply that similar approach to the Appellate Division.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: For the Appellate Division, parties will also have an option of consenting to a two-Judge coram to hear the appeal but that is subject to the approval of the Appellate Division.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, if both parties or all parties to an appeal consent, it can be heard by a two-Judge coram.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Second, the Bills expand the situations under which a civil appeal or application can be decided without hearing oral arguments.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: To be clear, the language that I have used – appeals refer to the substantive appeals itself, the applications are applications within the appeals that will arise but are not dispositive of the substantive merits of the appeal.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Presently, a civil appeal or application may be decided on paper in a number of limited situations.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: These situations are, first, an appeal against the decision of the SICC where all parties to the appeal consent; and second, any application to the Court of Appeal.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, again, party autonomy based on whether parties consent, then the Appellate Division and the Court of Appeal will have the ability to hear that on paper.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: These include appeals against interlocutory judgments and appeals against judgments relating to the assessment of damages.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, if all the parties agree, consent, it will be a two-Judge coram and to a paper hearing, then subject to the Appellate Division themselves considering that it is appropriate, then that can be a way in which that appeal can be resolved.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Third, the Appellate Division would also be able to decide any application brought before it without hearing oral arguments.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This will not require the consent of parties and is in line with the current practice of the Court of Appeal.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The possibility of paper hearings provides parties with an option, subject to the Court's approval, of having their matters resolved faster and at a lower cost.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This Bill simplifies the process for leave applications.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Currently, when leave is required to appeal against a decision, the leave application is usually heard by the Court that has made the decision being appealed against.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: If that Court declines to grant leave, a further application for leave can be made to the Appellate Court.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We will simplify this process, such as where leave is required to appeal against a decision of the General Division, the relevant Appellate Court will hear the application for leave.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The decision of the Appellate Court on the leave application will be final.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, what this amendment does is seek to increase the prospects of those types of cases being appealed, but with leave.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This amendment seeks to refine the balance between procedural efficiency and also fairness to the parties.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: There is also one amendment that we are considering in relation to the timing of when an application for further arguments will be taken.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Members will know that if you look at the proposed provision 29B(2a), the word that is being used here is "date".

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, the date by which one has to make the further arguments, versus the time by which one has to make the further arguments.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And we propose, at the Committee stage, with Mr Speaker and Chairman's leave, to seek to make that amendment.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It is a change that was not intended, an error carried through from the drafting.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, we propose to make that to reflect the position better.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And I think the lawyers in this House will appreciate that the use of the word "time" will give a greater degree of flexibility in terms of when one starts the computation of time for filing the further arguments.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, I will seek to make that amendment at the Committee stage.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Together, these amendments further enhance our judicial system, one that is already robust, flexible but now also allow for greater and more effective administration of justice.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My speech addresses the restructuring collectively proposed by all three Bills.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I support these amendments which will allow the Supreme Court to better manage its caseload in light of the increase in the number and complexity of cases.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I have just three clarifications on how the Court of Appeal will exercise its jurisdiction and how the restructuring will affect the application of existing case precedents.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The proposed section 29E(5) clarifies that the transfer may be made even if it is a case that is ordinarily allocated to the Court of Appeal.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Senior Minister of State clarify under what situations might the Court of Appeal make such a transfer?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Appendix B of the Ministry's press release on the restructuring of the Supreme Court suggests that the Court of Appeal may do so if the issues on appeal relate to settled law.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, what is settled law may not always be so clear cut.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For instance, the High Court in Public Prosecutor v Lam Leng Hung and others and the Court of Appeal in Public Prosecutor v Lam Leng Hung, more commonly known as the City Harvest cases, held that the directors did not fall within the definition of "agents" under section 409 of the Penal Code on criminal breach of trust by an agent.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In doing so, the Court of Appeal and the High Court overturned what had then seemed to be settled law for four decades that directors will be liable for the offence of criminal breach of trust by way of their businesses as agents in respect of property entrusted to them in the course of their duties as directors.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Admittedly, the City Harvest cases were criminal proceedings.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Nonetheless, the point stands that what appears to be settled law in civil proceedings may subsequently be contested.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The prescribed categories of civil appeals to be heard by the Court of Appeal are to be set out in a schedule, as the Senior Minister of State mentioned, to the amended SCJA and may be amended by the Minister after consulting the Chief Justice.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: While some flexibility is required, it would undermine the purpose of this categorisation and certainty for litigants if the Court of Appeal has unfettered discretion in determining which Court should hear the appeal.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Senior Minister of State provide some guidance on how the Court of Appeal should exercise its discretion under section 29E(1) in transferring a case ordinarily allocated to its jurisdiction to the Appellate Division?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, section 47(4) clarifies that the Court of Appeal is not required to grant leave even if the appeal will raise a point of law of public importance.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Senior Minister of State share what policy considerations override the benefit of having the Court of Appeal rule on a point of law of public importance?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In what categories of cases that raise a point of law of public importance should the Court of Appeal nonetheless decline to grant leave to appeal?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The doctrine of judicial precedent means that the finding of a higher Court which forms the basis of its decision is binding on a Court lower in the hierarchy.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Currently, the Court of Appeal is at the top of the hierarchy followed by the Singapore High Court, the District Court and the Magistrate's Court.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Appellate Division will effectively be the final appeals Court for many categories of civil matters and litigants may not have recourse to the Court of Appeal.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: How persuasive will the findings of the Appellate Division of the High Court be, compared against the findings of the current Court of Appeal before the restructuring takes place?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: These clarifications notwithstanding, I stand in support of all three Bills.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In summary, I understand the key proposed changes to be as follows.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Second, the channelling of cases to the new Appellate Division will free up the Court of Appeal to concentrate on appeals which are generally of wider public interest.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Under the proposed changes, all appeals from criminal cases originally heard by the High Court, will continue to go on appeal to the apex Court.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This is rightly so, as criminal cases heard by the High Court may involve sentences of life imprisonment or the death penalty and thus deserve scrutiny by the highest appellate Court.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: As for civil cases, there is also a list of certain types of civil cases that may still be appealed to the Court of Appeal from the High Court.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: While we have some queries on the details of the proposed changes, the Workers' Party is supportive of the rationale for the restructure of the Supreme Court.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: If the caseload is efficiently distributed, parties will have less waiting time for appeals, which must be a good thing.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Nevertheless, I wonder whether the Government has considered how the change might impact legal costs payable by parties.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In other words, will the introduction of a middle tier Appellate Division lead to cost escalation for appeals to the Court of Appeal, up from present levels?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: If so, this would be an unwelcome side-effect of the changes.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The Constitution (Amendment) Bill provides at clause 2 that there are various categories of persons holding "high judicial office", which is the position today.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Such persons are the Chief Justice, a Justice of the Court of Appeal, a Judge of the Appellate Division, a Judge of the High Court, a Judicial Commissioner, a Senior Judge or an International Judge.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For some of these categories of judicial officeholders, they are protected under Article 98(1) of the Constitution with security of tenure until age 65.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Other categories, however, like Judicial Commissioners and Senior Judges, are appointed for short terms of one to three years.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: As we have said in the past, in our view, having short-term judicial officeholders is not ideal.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Since we have debated this matter in the past, I shall keep my remarks on the principle short.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The judicial branch of the Government plays a vital role in the country's system of checks and balances between the Executive Government, the Legislature or Parliament, and the Judiciary.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The Courts are called upon to adjudicate disputes and must decide without fear or favour, regardless of who the parties are.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: To give assurance that the judicial branch is robust, security of tenure for judges is fundamental.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Just as Members of Parliament are accorded with Parliamentary Privilege to ensure free debate in this House, Judges are accorded the security of tenure till retirement age; it is further provided by the Constitution that the office of a Supreme Court Judge must not be abolished during the continuance in office of the Judge.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In 2014, when the post of senior judges was created, it was mentioned that retaining judges past their retirement age would enable tapping on their expertise.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In past debates, I do not recall the Government rejecting outright such a move and, today, I would like to give further grounds for this from a manpower utilisation perspective.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This suggestion for the retirement age of a Supreme Court Judge to be later than 65 is not radical.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: At the US Supreme Court, judges are appointed for life.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The current composition of the US Supreme Court includes two judges in their 80s, and the average age of the bench is about 67.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In Singapore, what is age 65 in today's context?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Singaporeans today have better health and longer lives.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Just looking around this House, there are several Members over 65, whom I need not name.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Nobody thinks they are incapable of rational thought or are losing their marbles.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: At the national level, data from the Ministry of Manpower shows that for 2018, the labour force participation rate of those aged between 65 and 69 is 45.3%, close to one in two persons.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: We see over 70s being cleaners and company directors.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In making this suggestion, it is not my intention to cast doubt on the integrity of those appointed as Judicial Commissioners or Senior Judges.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Neither are my observations directed at international judges, who may hold concurrent appointments in other jurisdictions and whose caseload revolves around international commercial disputes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: I wish to speak on the tenure of Supreme Court Judges.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Article 98 provides that they may not be removed from office except with cause, and even then, the recommendation of a tribunal of their peers is required.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Their terms of office, including remuneration, must not be altered to their disadvantage after appointment.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Such protections are vital to safeguard the separation of powers and the independence of the Judiciary.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Our Supreme Court Judges must decide cases that may adversely affect a sitting Government or the Legislature.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Their judgments may have great public and political impact.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: I wondered whether the retirement age of Supreme Court Judges in Singapore had been designed with an express Parliamentary intent.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: It seems that the retirement age Article originates in the Constitution (Amendment) Bill No 5 of 1969.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The Bill inserted after Article 52 of the Constitution, 52F on the tenure of office of Supreme Court Judges.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The original Article, and I quote, is: "Subject to the provisions of this Article, a judge of the Supreme Court shall hold office until he attains the age of sixty-five years or such later time not being later than six months after he attains that age, as the President may approve." The text has remained substantively the same since then.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The Explanatory Notes to the 1969 Bill state that this Article largely re-enacted the constitution of Malaysia's provisions on the Supreme Court, which were not present in the Constitution of Singapore.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Our Constitution, of course, was originally designed for Singapore as part of the Federation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: This was Minister for Law, Mr EW Barker's explanation to Parliament in the Second Reading debate on 12 June 1969.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: It seems that we have not then explicitly considered why the retirement age of Supreme Court judges is specified to be so.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: I note that the hon Member, Ms Sylvia Lim, has brought up this issue previously.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: I note also that the Malaysian constitution was amended in 2005 to raise the maximum age for a Supreme Court judge to 66 years.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The necessity to provide Supreme Court Judges with tenure and guaranteed terms of employment is not disputed.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: What is an issue is the basis for why the retirement age should be specified in the Constitution and is different from that applying to the rest of society.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: This may be viewed as inequitable anytime the age applying to the rest of society is lower or higher than that applying to Supreme Court Judges.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Of course, one key difference is that Supreme Court Judges are required to retire at that age, whereas workers outside are not.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: I think, more generally, there are at least two main purposes of having such an age limit.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: While our wisdom might increase in years, unfortunately, our cognitive functions do not.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The demands of high judicial office are exacting.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: It is obviously more graceful for a Supreme Court Judge to step down at the due time, than to be asked to retire on grounds of their loss of ability, or worse still, removed by a tribunal of their peers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: It also assures us that no party has any reason to complain on the basis of age affecting the quality of jurisprudence, which is specifically prohibited by Article 98 of the Constitution.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: In this regard, Supreme Court judges are not too different from citizens in other jobs, except for the lack of discretion in when to retire.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The other factor which may be qualitatively important or different is the risk of ossification of ideas or principles in jurisprudence that fail to reflect contemporary values.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Our formative years, our personal and professional experiences, contribute to the decisions that we make.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The central difficulty with those judicial systems that grant lifetime tenure, such as the Supreme Court of the US, is that the composition of the court becomes determined by the longevity of the individual Judges.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: This is not logical unless longevity itself is a judicial virtue.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: It is an issue even in a system with a set retirement age, such as ours, because the age of first appointment can vary both across individual Judges and across time.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: This means that the average tenure of a Supreme Court Judge can change even if the retirement age does not.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: If Judges are appointed early in their career, the end result can be a more ossified judicial system without any intent that this be so.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Therefore, it seems useful to consider: what are the aims of tenure of Supreme Court Judges?

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Why should the retirement age treat Supreme Court Judges differently from the rest of society?

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: What is a desirable length of tenure that protects Judges against political or public interference and yet mitigates the risk of ossification in jurisprudence?

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: If there is such a thing as an ideal tenure length, would it be better to appoint Supreme Court Judges for suitably long, fixed terms, rather than until a set retirement age?

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: I do not, of course, expect that these issues can be addressed directly in today's debate.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Perhaps a commission of suitable experts could consider these, amongst other issues, for the future.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But by drawing attention to this, I hope that future legislatures will consider the issue.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Historically, we have not considered it so much.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: We are not the only country to have to deal with this issue.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I am saying this bearing in mind that for any existing legislation hitherto requiring the Court of Appeal as the final Court hearing any appeal, it may still be possible to amend the relevant law, making the new Appellate Division as the final arbiter.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Yes, I am aware that the Senior Minister of State has provided some explanation in his opening speech and I thank him for that.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I do wonder whether the Senior Minister of State can elaborate a little further on this.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For example, how does the Government arrive at the conclusion that it would be suitable to have the Court of Appeal to hear cases under section 18(5) of the Maintenance of Parents Act and that it is not appropriate for such appeals to be now changed to, say, the Appellate Division instead.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The power to do so can be exercised inter alia on the Court of Appeal's own motion or on a reference by the Appellate Division.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Section 29(3) states that making a decision under section 29D(1) to so transfer the case to itself, the Court of Appeal must have regard to matters prescribed by the rules of the Court.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In addition to what the Senior Minister of State has shared with us earlier, I would like to ask him whether he is able to share a little bit more as to what would be these matters of considerations which the Ministry has in mind.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: They are instead appointed by the President with the concurring advice of the Prime Minister.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: A 2015 study by the Bingham Centre for the Rule of Law on the appointment, tenure and removal of judges in the Commonwealth found that such renewable appointments "place the career interest of a judge in conflict with the judicial responsibility for upholding the rule of law in cases involving the government or other powerful persons who may have influence over the renewal decision.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Such conflicts of interest may pose a risk to both the actual and perceived independence of the judiciary." Moreover, the reasons for offering contractual renewal to Judges no longer exist.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: I believe in the late 1960s, there was a serious shortage of High Court Judges, resulting in a backlog of Court cases.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Parliament allowed Judges beyond the retirement age of 65 to stay on as "contract Judges", enabling the judiciary to hold on to experienced and able Judges.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: This Senior Judge scheme is still in place today.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The Judicial Commissioner scheme was introduced in 1979 to attract top practitioners to be judges for a period between six months and three years, then go back to their practice.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The income disparity earned by judges and top practitioners was at that time very significant, so practitioners had to be financially attracted to become Judges.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: However, this changed in the mid-1990s when the salaries of Judges were raised by pegging them to top earners in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: These changes will enable the Judiciary to exercise the judicial power vested in them under Article 93 of our Constitution, free from encumbrances and worries that they may not be contractually renewed and, therefore, provide effective check and balance on the powers of the Executive and the Legislature.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Yet, the Parliamentary debates in this House rarely make reference to this supreme law.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Our Constitution delineates functions and powers of key public institutions, including the Legislature, the Executive, the Judiciary, and our Civil Service.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Amendments to the Constitution have also enabled significant tweaks to our political system, including the introduction of the Group Representation Constituency system, Nominated Members of Parliament system and the Elected Presidency, to operationalise.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Article 38 of our Constitution vests legislative power in the Legislature, which consists of the President and Parliament.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: This power enables us to shape our country's progress and our people's behaviours.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: How should we then exercise this power properly?

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: What are the constitutional ideals that we must uphold?

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Please allow me to outline three key roles.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: First, our Constitution provides for the existence of different branches of Government that serve as a check and balance on one another.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: While Parliament has legislative power, the Judiciary has judicial power, and the Cabinet has executive functions.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The Parliament vests powers of the Executive on persons other than the Cabinet, such as civil servants of high authority.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The Judiciary can make judgments on the constitutionality of legislation passed by Parliament.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The Judiciary can also make judgments on the failure of the Cabinet to properly exercise executive functions.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The Cabinet implements regulations and policies based on the legislation enacted by Parliament.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: It is, therefore, important for us to ensure that each branch has autonomy, so that they can fulfill these functions in the best possible way.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: This is the basis for my recommendation for security with tenure to ensure full judicial independence.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Second, we should strive to ensure the constitutionality of legislation for future judicial references.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: As the supreme law, all other laws passed must not contravene the Constitution.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Therefore, Article 4 provides that any law enacted by the Legislature which is inconsistent with this Constitution shall, to the extent of the inconsistency, be void.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: That would mean that in debating Bills, we should consider their consistency with our Constitution.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Such constitutionally-informed debates can protect the electorate's rights and allow public institutions like the judiciary to fulfill their roles, in full view of the electorate.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: I think we will all agree that this will help us build a more informed and engaged citizenry.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Termed fundamental liberties, they are meant to be zealously safeguarded, with Parliament only being able to restrict these liberties in very limited circumstances.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Hence, the legislation we enact must serve to protect these constitutionally-enshrined fundamental liberties, the Courts must also be enabled to protect these liberties by being duly kept independent.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: As we discuss the changes and significance of our judiciary system with this Bill and the importance of judicial independence with my earlier recommendation of tenure, I would like to seek your indulgence, Mr Speaker, to discuss a couple of policy examples where we could argue that judicial independence could guard against breaches on the constitutionality of legislation made, for example, to the equality provision.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I think what is at stake is really discussing the amendments of the Bill, amendments that are relevant to the Bill.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: I am demonstrating with the policy examples why the judicial independence is important, with my recommendation —

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: We recognise that, but I do not think we need to drag in other issues —

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: The other example I wanted to share is the debate on section 377A also —

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: If I can repeat myself, that we should keep to the amendments that are being discussed today.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: Our Constitution represented the dreams of a young democracy when it was first created with our sudden Independence and now bears the marks of the growth of a determined and thriving nation.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: We have come this far and won much praise for our world-class model of governance because of the strength of our Constitution in the separation of powers among the Judiciary, the Parliament and the Executive as well as the protection of the fundamental liberties of all Singaporeans, including the right to equality.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: We are in a stronger position than ever to keep fighting for these ideals so as to become the kind of society we want to be.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: For I do believe that the greatest threat to our Constitution would be our ignorance of it.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In my speech, I will focus on two areas: first, how the policy objective behind the creation of the new Appellate Division of the High Court is sought to be achieved; and second, the practical workings of some of the proposed new procedures set out in the SCJA.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Turning to the first point, I note that the reason for the proposal to create the new Court is to share the burgeoning appeals caseload between the existing Court of Appeal and the new Appellate Division of the High Court.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is expected to ensure that the Court processes remain efficient.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The hon Senior Minister of State had shared some statistics in relation to the heavy workload of the Court of Appeal in dealing with the appeals.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I do not wish to dwell at length about the reasons contributing to the increase, save as to point out that we all can agree that, as lawmakers, we have been passing quite a number of Bills both in the First and Second Sessions of the 13th Parliament and it does appear that our Ministers and their respective Ministries are not letting up and this rate of law-making may be likely to be maintained, if not go higher.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: So, eventually, all this would have an impact on the workload of the Judiciary which applies the law in accordance with the manifested intent of Parliament.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: A retired UK law lord, Lord Sumption, referred to this as "Law’s Expanding Empire".

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The proposed restructuring of the Judiciary to deal with the increase in the Appellate Court’s workload comes at a right time.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We need to ensure that the Judiciary, in its appellate jurisdiction, is provided with adequate resources so that the clearance rate is kept high, there is no significant backlog, and litigants get to receive their results of the cases within a reasonable time.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: At the same time, the quality of the judgments must be kept consistently high and in keeping with the hard-earned reputation for Singapore as a world-class, independent Court with exceptionally competent and committed Judges of the highest integrity.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In that regard, I noted the Senior Minister of State highlighting how well our Courts are rated in published rankings across the world.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: My learned friend Ms Sylvia Lim had highlighted a possibility of increased costs arising from the establishment of the Appellate Division of the High Court.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: But as I understand the workings of the system, for at least the overwhelming majority of the cases, it is not to have a two-tier appeal.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: For the overwhelming majority of cases, you only have a one-tier appeal.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Only in cases where there are novel points of law of public importance will there be a second set of appeal to the Court of Appeal.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: And that is rightly so because the Court of Appeal is the apex Court.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: So, in that regard, I think the impact of cost should not be very significant.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It is also expected to become heavier for the reasons I just mentioned.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: How can we ensure that the workload of the High Court is dealt with by an adequate number of Judges?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I acknowledge that it is also not easy to appoint Judges, given that Singapore is a small country with a limited pool of legal talent.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It is not easy to find top talent with the right aptitude for public service to agree to be appointed as Supreme Court Judges.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I would welcome the Senior Minister of State's response on my query.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Several Members, including Ms Anthea Ong and Assoc Prof Walter Theseira, talked about increasing the retirement age of Judges.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I am not sure whether that is an appropriate suggestion because there is a linkage between increasing retirement age and independence of the Judiciary.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: But I see this as two separate things.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Based on how the Judges have been appointed, the appointment of Senior Judges as well as Judicial Commissioners are done on an ad hoc basis to clear workload as and when workload increases.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: And I think that flexibility must still be retained.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: But I think we should be careful about drawing an analogy between these Judges who are there for specific reasons to clear workload and then an inference that somehow the independence of the Judiciary is affected by their appointments.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I now turn to the other proposed amendments in the Bills.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: First, the configuration of the High Court hearing a civil case in the proposed General Division.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The proposed section 10(1) of SCJA stipulates that proceedings in the General Division of the High Court dealing with civil cases should be before a single Judge.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is the same requirement that exists now.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I note, however, section 18G of SCJA allows the SICC, which is another division of the High Court dealing with international commercial cases, allowing for proceedings to be heard before a single or three Judges.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The reason for having three Judges, amongst others, is a recognition of the complexity of the cases that SICC would have to deal with.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It may be good to give the Court the discretion to decide which number is more appropriate, having regard to all the facts and circumstances.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I would be grateful for the Senior Minister of State’s views on this matter.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Second, I note that there is a list of situations set out in the proposed Sixth Schedule where appeals are brought directly to the Court of Appeal, instead of the Appellate Division.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I reviewed the list and I note that under paragraph 1(i) of the Sixth Schedule, there is a raft of legislation, from the Administration of Justice (Protection) Act to the Competition Act to Maintenance of Parents Act dealing with a diverse range of topics in respect of which it is stipulated that appeals are to be brought to the Court of Appeal.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This would prevent controversy from arising once this Bill is passed and put into effect.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Next, I note that the proposed section 29D of SCJA provides that the Court of Appeal may transfer a right of appeal against an order made under a provision in the Land Acquisition Act.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In this regard, I note that section 29(2) of the Land Acquisition Act provides for an appeal to the Court of Appeal from the decision of the Board on questions of law.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: What is the special characteristic of this provision, section 39(A) in the Land Acquisition Act which, for some reason, I am unable to find in the statute book?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Under the proposed section 29E of SCJA, the Court of Appeal may transfer an appeal made under the Land Acquisition Act to the Appellate Division.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Given that the legislative intent under the Land Acquisition Act is for the Court of Appeal to hear these cases, may I know what are the circumstances in which such remission is proposed so that it is made in a way that coheres with Parliamentary intent?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I believe the learned Senior Minister of State mentioned something about the situation where all the substantive issues are dealt with, dealing only with ancillary matters.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Perhaps that could be a situation that is being contemplated.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Next, it is proposed under Schedule 7 of SCJA that there are certain categories of cases which may be heard by a Judge or two Judges of the Appellate Division.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This arrangement is different from the current Sixth Schedule which specifically states the circumstances in which the Court of Appeal will have a single Judge or when it will have two Judges.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Also, who will decide how many Judges would sit in these circumstances?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The learned Senior Minister of State mentioned about a configuration of Judges based on consent of parties.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Is that what is being suggested in these provisions?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: My questions will also apply to similar provisions that are proposed to be applicable to the Court of Appeal.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Next, Civil Jurisdiction of the Appellate Division is specifically provided under the proposed section 31 and 35 of SCJA that the Appellate Division only has civil jurisdiction.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Disciplinary cases brought in the Supreme Court are quasi-criminal in nature but generally invoke civil procedure.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Next, dealing with appeals from the Appellate Division to the Court of Appeal, I note that leave is required; and it makes eminent sense for leave to be required, otherwise the whole rationale of dividing the workload would be thwarted.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I am also grateful to Mr Murali Pillai for his well wishes and also for his wide-ranging speech where he answered not just some other Members' questions, but also some of his own.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Ms Sylvia Lim asked whether the cost of appeal to the Court of Appeal would escalate given the introduction of the Appellate Division as a middle tier.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I go back to my earlier point that the Appellate Division is not to be seen as a middle tier.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In general, it will not add a further level of appeal in the vast majority of cases, and it is not a level of appeal that has to be crossed before one gets to the Court of Appeal.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The appeals from the General Division will be allocated in the first instance.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, Members heard me say earlier that there will be two tracks, one of which goes direct to the Court of Appeal and the rest goes to the Appellate Division.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Any further appeal from the Appellate Division will require leave.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Murali Pillai, I think, answered that question, and leave will only be granted in very limited situations.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In most cases, parties will not go through an additional tier of appeal after a decision from the General Division.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: As is the case today, there will, therefore, generally be only one tier of appeal.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The amendments before the House today also contain initiatives to lower costs of litigation for parties, to address Ms Sylvia Lim's point directly.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, either by way of paper hearing, which will be quicker and also less expensive in the context of some cases.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But all that is, of course, subject to the overriding discretion of the Court's assessment that it is appropriate for the administration of justice in a case for parties to proceed on a paper hearing.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Louis Ng asked how the restructuring of the Supreme Court would affect the doctrine of judicial precedent, or stare decisis.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In line with the usual principles of stare decisis, decisions of the higher Court are binding on the lower Court.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Decisions of the Court of Appeal will, therefore, have precedence over decisions of the Appellate Division.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This is regardless of whether the decision in question has been issued before or after the establishment of the Appellate Division.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The decision of the Appellate Division will be binding on the General Division and the lower Courts.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And the existing High Court decisions will not bind the new Appellate Division.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: They will have instead the same weight as a decision from the General Division after it is set up.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Dennis Tan and Mr Murali Pillai asked about the categories of appeals in the Sixth Schedule – how they are chosen, what was the thought process going into it.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Murali Pillai also asked about the Land Acquisition Act.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: These will also be ordinarily allocated to the Court of Appeal.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In my opening speech, I outlined the key considerations for allocating the categories of cases to the Court of Appeal directly.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Just to quickly recap, these include cases which will have a likely substantial consequence for the individual or society, have involved significant public interest questions which will benefit from the guidance of the Court of Appeal, possibly also novel questions of law, complex cases and so on.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It was Mr Dennis Tan, I believe, who raised the questions specifically on section 18(5) of the Maintenance of Parents Act.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: If Mr Dennis Tan looks at that section, it specifically provides for an appeal on the basis of public interest.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I think one can understand why an issue which the Maintenance of Parents Act covers might be something that one channels directly to the Court of Appeal.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Importantly, however, for Members to note, the ordinary allocation of appeals, whilst there is a default, is not rigid.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The categories allocated to the Court of Appeal are also not cast in stone.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: For example, as I said in my opening speech, should there be novel questions that we put into the categories today, they may be resolved or settled with the passage of time.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Those cases can eventually come off that list if it can be dealt with by the Appellate Division.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: If an initial area of law is more established or there is a new area of law, that can also be added to the categories.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Next, let me touch on the transfer powers of the Court of Appeal.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Louis Ng, Mr Dennis Tan and Mr Murali Pillai touched on them and raised some questions.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: As a starting point, the allocation of matters in the two tracks that I mentioned will apply generally, as a starting position.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: However, it is useful beyond the default allocation to allow the Court of Appeal themselves looking at the specific case and understanding the issues that are raised beyond just the label that is put on it, a discretion to transfer to itself or to the Appellate Division depending on its assessment of complexity, novelty and so on.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The basis on which it seeks to do so – novelty, complexity, cases of general public importance and so on – would be amongst the factors that will guide the exercise of discretion in any such transfer exercise.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: At the same time, the powers of the Court of Appeal in doing so are not unfettered, and Members will note clauses 29D(3), 29E(3) and 47(3) of the amended SCJA which expressly require that the Court of Appeal have regard to the matters prescribed in the Rues of Court when exercising these powers.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: As I had mentioned, the relevant matters will be prescribed in the Rules of Court.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Murali Pillai asked specifically about the Land Acquisition Act.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The land acquisition appeals currently lie from the Land Appeals Board.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: They do not lie from the General Division up to either Appellate Division or the Court of Appeal but lie from the Appeals Board.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, for that reason, they are set out separately from the Sixth Schedule which applies only to civil appeals from the General Division.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Murali Pillai also asked what are the principles of that remission, and that is one of the questions that you answered yourself.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: On a related note, Mr Louis Ng asked about the transfer to the Appellate Division should the case raise a matter of settled law.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Louis Ng's point seems to be that where a case might appear settled or uncontroversial, the law may subsequently nonetheless be overturned.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, the question is how do we then determine that upfront?

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The reality is that in most cases, it will be clear if there are controversial points of law that ought to be decided by the Court of Appeal, and that would be flagged earlier rather than later.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: For example, when settled law is challenged by a party on appeal, the party first has to give notice of its position, file its case, outline its arguments, and the Court would be able to appreciate those arguments upfront.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Further, in deciding whether to transfer an appeal, the Court of Appeal, of course, will also have regard to all the relevant circumstances, including the party's case which I have set out and raised earlier on and, of course, understand the nature of the case.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: As Members who practise in the Courts know, the Courts very actively conduct pre-trial conferences to understand the nature of the parties’ dispute, understand the ambit of the disagreement, and to understand whether this would involve novel questions of law, or whether the parties are seeking a question to be overturned on a settled point of law.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Nonetheless, despite all that, where the appeal has been transferred to the Appellate Division and, in the course of that hearing, an unanticipated issue of law of public importance, novelty, complexity arises, the matter can still go on appeal to the Court of Appeal with leave.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Louis Ng and Mr Murali Pillai raised questions about the power of the Court of Appeal to decline to grant leave for a further appeal from the Appellate Division to the Court of Appeal, even if a point of law of public importance is raised.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: However, as Members would appreciate, this alone would not be sufficient as a criterion to grant leave of appeal.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Other matters in the interest of the administration of justice were also considered.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Whether or not there should be further appeal should take into account the fact that the parties had had already a chance to raise their arguments, and nothing new is coming through in the application for leave to appeal.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: They raised the arguments before the Appellate Division, and the Appellate Division has reviewed them and decided on that point of law.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In other jurisdictions, it is not always sufficient as well just to rely on a point of law of public importance to seek and obtain permission for leave to appeal and I will just cite one example.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In Australia, section 35A of Australia's Judiciary Act provides that the High Court of Australia may, when determining whether to grant special leave to appeal, "have regard to any matters that it considers relevant" and that this shall include not only whether the appeal involves a question of law of public importance, but also other factors, such as whether the interests of justice require it.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, there is a degree of flexibility in the discretion given to the judge to assess a particular case and to assess whether, on top of the question of public importance, there are other reasons in the dispensation of justice for this to be heard on appeal.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Rather, this is heard by the Court of Three Judges; I think doctors as well.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This remains unchanged by the introduction of the Appellate Division.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Murali Pillai touched on the minimum composition of the Appellate Division and the Court of Appeal in cases that may be heard by fewer than three Judges.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Specifically, he raised the difference in the arrangement of the Sixth Schedule in the existing SCJA – I think the Member said – and the corresponding Seventh Schedule of this Bill.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: For example, if there is a matter that is currently only heard by a minimum of two Judges, that will remain the case in the Bill.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, the Bill does not seek to change those arrangements.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: On SICC, Mr Murali Pillai asked about the difference in the number of Judges.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Because there are unique considerations behind the SICC.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Although it is a Division of the current High Court and will be a Division as well like the General Division after the amendments, they apply to cases of international commercial considerations and they also have a panel of specialist commercial judges comprising not only Singapore Supreme Court Judges but also International Judges from a myriad of different landscapes, backgrounds and also legal systems.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The strength and diversity of the panel are key advantages to attract parties to submit international disputes before SICC, especially where the issues in dispute relate to foreign law or commercial practices in key jurisdictions overseas.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We wish to correct the word "date" to "time" and I wish to also clarify with Mr Murali Pillai that there is no missing word in between the two sub-provisions.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I think, to be very careful, in different shades, Assoc Prof Walter Theseira, Ms Sylvia Lim and Ms Anthea Ong have raised the point.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: There are a couple of questions: first, on the retirement age; second, on the tenure of Judges being extended to the age of 70; and finally – I think that is Assoc Prof Walter Theseira's point – on what is the desired tenure.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I think that was the point he made and whether there should be a fixed period.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In essence, these questions – save for Assoc Prof Walter Theseira's which I will address – relate to that of the independence of our Judiciary: one of tenure and one of retirement age.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: First, by borrowing from Mr Murali Pillai's own speech where he answered the point by explaining that these are effectively two different things – to look at tenure and to look at the retirement ages of the Judges are two different things when you look at the issue of independence.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The Government regards a strong and trusted Judiciary as the bedrock of the rule of law.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This is the point that has been made by the Minister for Law previously and it is a point that is worth reiterating in the context of the points raised in this debate.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The question then is, what does success look like for our Judiciary?

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Because ultimately – whatever you might say about the retirement age, the tenure – the key question is, how successful?

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: What benefits do we have from a strong, trusted Judiciary, an effective trusted Judiciary which is able to attract and retain the best legal talent that we have and which operates in a climate where there are no extraneous factors, no influences interfering with the ability of the Judges to perform their jobs?

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The question is: have we achieved that outcome?

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It is a number but what does that mean?

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: One integral aspect of the rule of law is an independent Judiciary which makes decisions based on facts and law and without regard to extraneous factors.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, clearly, we can see from the rankings that judicial independence in Singapore is strong and consistently so.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: You look at the UK, where judges there have tenure until the age of 70.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: As you know, in 2016, there was this UK Attitude Survey.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It was a stark reminder of how things could quickly go wrong if we are not careful.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Forty-three percent of judges felt valued by the public.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Seventy-four percent of judges felt that the remuneration does not adequately reflect the work they do.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Sixty-one percent said opportunities for career progression was important but support for this was either non-existent or poor.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Forty-seven percent of high court judges and forty-one percent of court of appeal judges – and these are judges in the UK system – said they intended to leave the Judiciary in the next five years.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Two percent of judges felt valued by the government.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: As I have said, these are survey numbers.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But they, overall, give you a sense and picture and they show that there is a system that is facing a serious problem of morale, recruitment and retention.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, is this a system which has tenure till 70 a better system?

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: That is why I go back to Mr Murali Pillai's point.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It is not about what age we ask the Judges to retire at and what tenure we give the Judges, but it is in the quality of the output and the quality of the performance that we measure our success.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, whilst I do not disagree with Members that the broader philosophical issues on security of tenure, of course, the linkage to independence and so on are important, we must never lose sight of the practical factors that have allowed us to build a first-class Judiciary that we now have.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We want to always ensure that the morale of the Judiciary remains high, that it continues to attract and retain persons of the highest calibre, legal talent of the highest scruples, so that the highest levels of public trust can be maintained.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Trust and respect in the Judiciary have been carefully and closely built up over the generations – and I think Members will agree – it has to be zealously guarded, for it can be easily lost if we are not careful.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In Singapore, when we first introduced retirement age laws in 1993, employers were not allowed to ask employees to retire before 60.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
